introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Geography 2 (0550), Paper 2, ORDINARY LEVEL, JUNE 2023. Duration: Two and a Half (2 1/2) hours.**

Instructions to candidates:

- Answer FOUR Questions choosing ONE from each section.
- Question ONE carries 30 marks. All the other Questions carry 20 marks each.
- Each question that is sub-divided has the sub marks in brackets.
- In questions involving calculations, all steps of the working MUST be shown.
- If an outline MAP and/or GRAPH are used, they must be tied inside your answer booklet, opposite the written part of the answer.
- NB - ONLY THE FIRST FOUR QUESTIONS ANSWERED WILL BE MARKED.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(a) Study the Ordnance Survey map Extract of Barmouth (1:50.000) provided and answer the following questions:

Reduce the map to half the original scale and insert the following:

(i) The limit of the National Nature Reserve.

(ii) River Afon Dysynni from 710093 to 650081.

(iii) A railway line.

(iv) The highland area southeast of River Afon Dysynni and Tal-Llyn-Lake.

(v) The lake at 657117.

(vi) The parking at 697 154.

Add a key and a new scale.

[12 marks]
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Step 1: the new scale.** The original scale is 1:50 000, so 2 cm on the map stand for 1 km on the ground. To reduce the map to **half its size**, every length is divided by 2, so the new scale is 1:100 000 and **1 cm stands for 1 km**.

- Ground area of the extract: 8 km by 13 km.
- Original map: $8 \times 2 = 16$ cm by $13 \times 2 = 26$ cm.
- Reduced map: $16 \div 2 = 8$ cm by $26 \div 2 = 13$ cm.

**Step 2: frame and grid.** Draw a rectangle 8 cm wide and 13 cm high. Rule the grid lines every 1 cm (each square is still 1 km by 1 km) and give them the same numbers as on the original map: 65 to 73 along the bottom (eastings) and 07 to 20 up the side (northings).

**Step 3: insert the features.** For a six-figure grid reference, the position from the lower left corner of the new map is $x = (\text{easting} - 65)$ cm to the right and $y = (\text{northing} - 07)$ cm upwards.

| Feature | Grid reference and what to copy from the map | Position on the new map | Symbol |
|---|---|---|---|
| (i) Limit of the National Nature Reserve | The reserve is named on the map near 7213 (Cadair Idris National Nature Reserve). Trace the boundary line printed round the Cadair Idris massif, which includes Llyn Cau and the summit ridge, in the east and south-east of the middle of the extract. | about 5 to 8 cm across and 4 to 7 cm up (copy the printed boundary) | dashed boundary line |
| (ii) River Afon Dysynni, 710093 to 650081 | Starts near Tal-y-llyn (710093), flows south-west along the valley floor beside the road, passes near Cedris Farm (about 688082) and leaves the extract at the western edge near 650081. | start (6.0, 2.3) cm; Cedris Farm about (3.8, 1.2) cm; end (0.0, 1.1) cm | blue line with a flow arrow towards the south-west |
| (iii) A railway line | The map shows a dismantled railway on the shore of the Mawddach estuary (printed in abbreviated form, near 705186, and continuing south-west along the shore as a walking route). Any railway line shown on the map is accepted. | e.g. from (5.5, 11.6) cm towards the west | black line with cross ticks, noted as dismantled in the key |
| (iv) The highland area south-east of the Dysynni and Tal-y-llyn Lake | The upland of Craig Goch, Mynydd Cedris and Mynydd Rugog (spot height 574 m), in the south-east corner of the extract. | about 5 to 8 cm across and 0 to 2.5 cm up | brown shading or hachures, named |
| (v) The lake at 657117 | Llyn Cyri, on the west side of the extract. | (0.7, 4.7) cm | blue outline, named |
| (vi) The parking at 697 154 | The parking symbol (P) beside the road near Islawrdref, next to the public convenience (PC). | (4.7, 8.4) cm | the printed parking sign (white P on a blue square) |

**Step 4: the key.** List every symbol you drew with its meaning: nature reserve boundary, river, railway (dismantled), highland, lake, parking. Keep the same symbols as the printed key.

**Step 5: the new scale.** Write the statement of scale (1 cm to 1 km), the representative fraction (1:100 000) and draw a linear scale: a line 5 cm long marked 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 km, with the first kilometre divided into tenths. Add a title and the north arrow.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(b) Calculate the area between the main road A496 and A493; (show all steps in the working).

[4 marks]
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Method.** On a 1:50 000 map one grid square measures 2 cm by 2 cm, which is 1 km by 1 km on the ground, so **1 grid square = 1 km$^2$**.

1. Find the two roads. The A496 is the northern main road (Cherdeon, Bontddu, Pen-y-bryn, Llanelltyd). The A493 is the southern main road (the edge of the extract near 6516, Abergwynant, Penmaenpool, then east to join the A496 near Llanelltyd). Between them lies the Mawddach estuary and its shores.
2. Close the area: the roads meet in the east (squares 7118 to 7218) and the western limit is the edge of the map (grid line 65).
3. Take the area strip by strip, one column of squares at a time (whole squares count 1, squares more than half inside count 1, squares less than half inside are ignored, or add up halves). Reading the map, the width of the area between the roads, in km, is about:

| Column of squares | 65-66 | 66-67 | 67-68 | 68-69 | 69-70 | 70-71 | 71-72 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Width between the roads (km) | 2.4 | 2.1 | 1.8 | 1.1 | 0.9 | 0.9 | 0.5 |

4. Add up: $\text{Area} = 2.4 + 2.1 + 1.8 + 1.1 + 0.9 + 0.9 + 0.5 = 9.7 \text{ km}^2$ (each column is 1 km wide, so width $\times$ 1 km = area).

**Answer: about 9.7 km$^2$** (an answer of roughly 9 to 10 km$^2$ is acceptable, because the result depends on how the squares are counted). Always give the unit and show the counting.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(c) (i) What is the relationship between the distribution of roads and relief?

[6 marks]

(ii) Comment on the drainage of the map.

[4 marks]
questions.corrige_markdown:
**(i) Roads and relief.** The roads follow the low ground and avoid the high, steep land.

- **The main roads keep to the valley floors and shores.** The A496 follows the north shore of the Mawddach estuary and the A493 follows the south shore. The spot heights printed beside the A493 are small (25 m, 37 m, 43 m near Abergwynant), while the hills above it rise to over 300 m. The road beside Tal-y-llyn Lake (the B4405, with the spot heights 82 m and 94 m) also runs along the valley floor.
- **Roads follow the direction of the relief.** The valleys and ridges run from north-east to south-west, and the A493, the road to Tal-y-llyn and the road along the Dysynni valley all run in the same direction, along the foot of the slopes, bending with the contours.
- **The highland has almost no roads.** Around Cadair Idris (spot heights 893 m and 855 m on Mynydd Moel) there are only footpaths and tracks (for example the Fox's Path and the Minffordd Path), shown by broken lines. Steep slopes, crags and corries make road building too difficult and costly.
- **Roads are linked to settlement.** The villages (Bontddu, Penmaenpool, Tal-y-llyn, Llanfihangel-y-pennant) are strung along the roads in the lowlands. Where a road must cross the river it uses a bridge (for example near Pont Ystumanner).

**Conclusion:** the distribution of roads is controlled by relief: dense, important roads in the valleys and along the coastal estuary, very few in the mountain area.

**(ii) Drainage.**

- **Main rivers:** the Afon Dysynni flows south-west from Tal-y-llyn Lake down its valley, and the Afon Mawddach widens into a tidal estuary in the north (flowing west towards the sea).
- **Many streams and lakes in the upland:** numerous small streams run down the slopes of Cadair Idris, so the drainage density is high on the steep ground. Lakes lie in hollows: Llyn Cau, Llyn y Gadair, Llyn Gafr, Llyn Gwernan, Llyn Cyri and Tal-y-llyn Lake.
- **Pattern:** streams flow away from the high ground in several directions (north towards the Mawddach, south-west and south towards the Dysynni, east towards Tal-y-llyn), a rough radial pattern around the Cadair Idris massif, joined by tributaries in a tree-like (dendritic) pattern.
- **Features:** waterfalls are named on the map (for example near 7212 and 6907), which shows steep stream courses; the lowland stretches are flatter and the river is wider with meanders.
- **Overall:** the area is well drained, with a high density of streams in the highland and few streams on the lowland.

questions.enonce_markdown:
(d) With map evidence state any FOUR functions of the Town of Barmouth.

[4 marks]
questions.corrige_markdown:
The built-up area visible on the extract is at the eastern edge (about squares 7118 to 7218), where buildings, roads and a road junction are close together. Any four functions with map evidence:

1. **Tourism and recreation:** hotels and inns (for example at Penmaenpool, Bontddu and Tal-y-llyn), parking places (the P signs), the Nature Information Centre, picnic and viewpoint signs, and footpaths and walks into the Cadair Idris National Nature Reserve.
2. **Residential:** a dense cluster of buildings and a network of streets in the town, with villages such as Bryn-y-gwin and Dolrhyd around it.
3. **Transport and route centre:** the A496 and the A493 meet near the town, with bridges, a toll crossing at Penmaenpool, and the line of a dismantled railway along the estuary.
4. **Services (commercial and public):** hotels, public conveniences (PC) and a school (marked Sch) near the built-up area, which serve the surrounding villages.
5. (Extra) **Quarrying:** old quarries (marked dis for disused) lie on the hill slopes of the area, for example near 6515 and 7014.

A good answer names each function and quotes the evidence (symbol, name or grid reference).
